title: Sheets are a System: 5 Rules for Better UX
summary: This reel explains the fundamental differences between sheets and modals, providing five specific rules for designing effective sheets. It covers context preservation, snap points, velocity-based dismissal, desktop responsiveness, and the importance of replacing content rather than stacking sheets.

transcript.text: One action. Modal, bottom sheet, side drawer. Only one fits.
A sheet keeps the page visible. A modal hides it behind a scrim.
Need the order while you edit the address? Sheet.
Need a full stop, like deleting the account? Modal. That is the whole decision.
A sheet never sits at a random height. Three snap points: peek, half, full.
Peek shows a summary. Half gives you the form. Full takes over for long content. Let go between two, it springs to the nearest.
Drag to dismiss reads speed, not distance. A quick flick closes it from anywhere. A slow drag needs to cross the halfway line. Distance alone makes the sheet feel stuck.
On desktop, the sheet turns into a side drawer. Minimum 320 pixels or the form breaks. Maximum 40% of the screen or it becomes a page. The list stays readable next to it.
Never stack two sheets. Tapping a saved address inside a sheet? Replace the content, add a back arrow. One sheet, one swipe to leave.

Five rules. One container that keeps the page in view. Now make Claude Code think like a senior UX designer. UX Engine designs the screen before coding, audits what is broken, reviews the diff, and kills the AI look. Link in bio.

on_screen_text: Keep the page, or stop it.
design_principles: Context Preservation: Sheets keep the background visible while modals use a scrim to focus on a single action.
Snap Points: Sheets should snap to predefined heights (peek, half, full) rather than free-floating.
Velocity-based Dismissal: Interaction should prioritize flick speed over drag distance for closing.
Responsive Constraints: Side drawers on desktop should be bounded between 320px and 40% screen width.
Content Replacement: Avoid stacking multiple sheets; replace internal content and use back navigation instead.
before_after: Contrasts incorrect sheet implementations (free-floating heights, distance-only dismissal, and stacked sheets) with a systematic approach using snap points, velocity thresholds, and content replacement.
